q: This Dutch scientist, using hand-made microscopes with a single lens, was the first to observe bacteria and protozoa, which he called "animalcules." He also observed red blood cells and spermatozoa. For 10 points, name this "father of microbiology."

These two brothers from Ohio flew the first powered, controlled, heavier-than-air aircraft at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, in 1903. They ran a bicycle shop in Dayton. For 10 points, name these aviation pioneers named Orville and Wilbur.

This gene-editing technique, adapted from a bacterial immune system, uses a guide RNA to direct a nuclease to a specific DNA sequence. Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier received the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing it. For 10 points, name this technique whose name has a Cas9 enzyme.

This New Zealand-born physicist, called the father of nuclear physics, discovered alpha and beta radiation and proposed that atoms have a small dense nucleus after his gold foil experiment. He won the 1908 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. For 10 points, name this scientist.

This African American mathematician worked at NASA, where she calculated orbital trajectories for the Mercury and Apollo missions by hand. John Glenn asked that she personally verify the computer's numbers for his 1962 orbital flight. She is one of the women featured in the book and film Hidden Figures. For 10 points, name this mathematician.

q: This English fossil collector from Lyme Regis found early ichthyosaur and plesiosaur skeletons in the cliffs along the Jurassic Coast. Despite being excluded from the scientific societies of her day because she was a working-class woman, her finds influenced ideas of extinction. A tongue twister about seashells is often said to be about her. For 10 points, name this paleontologist.

This Austrian-born economist's The Road to Serfdom argued that central planning leads to tyranny. He criticized Keynes and shared the 1974 Nobel Prize with Gunnar Myrdal. For 10 points, name this author of The Use of Knowledge in Society, first name Friedrich.

This British economist's 1936 book The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money argued that insufficient aggregate demand can cause prolonged unemployment, justifying government spending. For 10 points, name this economist.

This University of Chicago economist, author of Capitalism and Freedom, led the school of monetarism, arguing that inflation is "always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon." For 10 points, name this Nobel winner, first name Milton.

This curve, named for a New Zealand-born economist, plotted a historical inverse relationship between unemployment and wage inflation in Britain. Friedman and Phelps argued it breaks down in the long run. For 10 points, name this curve, named for A. W. Phillips.

This curve plots the cumulative share of income against the cumulative share of population. The area between it and the line of perfect equality is used to compute the Gini coefficient. For 10 points, name this curve named for Max Lorenz.

The Laffer curve, popularized in the 1970s, suggests that there is a tax rate that maximizes this quantity, because a tax rate of 100 percent would collect none. For 10 points, name this item collected by governments.

This type of good, named for a Scottish economist, is an inferior good whose quantity demanded rises when its price rises, as in the case of staple foods among the very poor. For 10 points, name this paradoxical good.

This theorem, named for a Nobel winner at the University of Chicago, says that if transaction costs are low, parties can bargain to an efficient outcome regardless of the initial assignment of property rights. For 10 points, name this theorem named for Ronald.

This concept, named for an Italian engineer-economist, describes an allocation in which no one can be made better off without making someone else worse off. For 10 points, name this standard of efficiency.

This English economist's 1817 book Principles of Political Economy and Taxation developed the theory of comparative advantage using the example of cloth and wine in England and Portugal. For 10 points, name this man, first name David.

In the 1970 paper "The Market for Lemons," this economist showed that asymmetric information can cause markets for used cars to collapse. He shared the 2001 Nobel Prize with Michael Spence and Joseph Stiglitz. For 10 points, name this man, first name George.

This term names a situation where one party in a transaction has more or better information than the other, and which leads insurers to attract riskier customers. Its counterpart in insurance is moral hazard. For 10 points, name this problem.

This Austrian-American economist's Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy described "creative destruction," the process by which innovation topples old industries. For 10 points, name this man, first name Joseph.
This 1944 conference in New Hampshire created the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank and set up a system of fixed exchange rates pegged to the dollar. For 10 points, name this conference.

This 1930 United States law raised tariffs on over twenty thousand imports and was followed by foreign retaliation, worsening the Great Depression. For 10 points, name this law named for a senator and a representative.

In macroeconomics, this empirical relationship, named for a Yale economist, says that a one-point rise in cyclical unemployment corresponds to a drop of about two points in GDP growth relative to potential. For 10 points, name this law named for Arthur.

This model, developed by Robert Solow and Trevor Swan, explains economic growth through capital accumulation, labor growth and technological progress. It predicts convergence. For 10 points, name this growth model.
This rule, named for a Stanford economist, suggests that a central bank should set its interest rate based on inflation and the output gap. For 10 points, name this guideline named for John.
This condition, named for Keynes, occurs when interest rates are near zero and monetary policy loses its ability to stimulate the economy, because people hoard cash. For 10 points, name this trap.

This economist's theorem proved that no ranking system for three or more options can satisfy a small set of reasonable criteria simultaneously, such as non-dictatorship. For 10 points, name this Nobel laureate, first name Kenneth.
In this game theory concept, named for a mathematician portrayed in A Beautiful Mind, no player can improve their outcome by changing strategy alone. For 10 points, name this kind of equilibrium.

This game, popularized by Albert Tucker, involves two prisoners who each can cooperate or defect. The dominant strategy for each is to defect, even though both would be better off cooperating. For 10 points, name this classic game theory problem.

This hypothesis, developed by the Chicago economist Eugene Fama, says that asset prices fully reflect available information, so it is impossible to consistently beat the market. For 10 points, name this hypothesis, abbreviated EMH.

Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky developed this theory in 1979, in which people evaluate gains and losses relative to a reference point and feel losses more strongly. For 10 points, name this behavioral alternative to expected utility theory.

This ecologist's 1968 essay describes a pasture open to all in which each herder adds animals until the resource is ruined. Elinor Ostrom later challenged the pessimistic conclusion. For 10 points, name this concept, a "tragedy of the" shared land.

This 1933 United States law separated commercial banking from investment banking and created federal deposit insurance. It was largely repealed in 1999. For 10 points, name this law named for a senator and a representative.

This term describes the damage to a country's manufacturing sector when a resource boom, like gas discoveries in the Netherlands in the 1960s, leads to currency appreciation. For 10 points, name this phenomenon, named for a Western European country.

This Chicago economist's work on rational expectations argued that predictable policy changes will not affect real output, since people anticipate them. His critique is named for him. For 10 points, name this Nobel laureate, first name Robert.
This index, created by The Economist in 1986, compares prices of a burger around the world as an informal test of purchasing power parity. For 10 points, name this lighthearted index.

This Scottish philosopher's 1776 book The Wealth of Nations introduced the metaphor of the "invisible hand" and described how the division of labor, illustrated by a pin factory, raises productivity. For 10 points, name this author, first name Adam.

q: This psychologist founded the first experimental psychology laboratory at the University of Leipzig in 1879. He used introspection to study the elements of consciousness, an approach called structuralism by his student Edward Titchener. For 10 points, name this German pioneer, whose name is Wilhelm.

After winning a Nobel Prize in 1904 for his research on digestive glands, this Russian scientist turned to the reflex now named for him. He noticed that dogs salivated when they heard a metronome or bell that had been paired with food. For 10 points, name this founder of classical conditioning.

This Harvard psychologist invented an operant conditioning chamber, nicknamed a box for him, and wrote Walden Two and Beyond Freedom and Dignity. He studied reinforcement schedules using pigeons and rats. For 10 points, name this radical behaviorist, first name B. F.

This psychologist founded behaviorism in a 1913 manifesto and conducted the Little Albert experiment with Rosalie Rayner. He later became an advertising executive. For 10 points, name this American, first name John B.

In this 1961 experiment by Albert Bandura, children watched an adult hit an inflatable clown and later imitated the aggression. It demonstrated social learning. For 10 points, name this experiment, named for a toy.

In these 1961 experiments at Yale, participants gave what they thought were increasingly severe electric shocks to a learner when told to continue by an experimenter in a lab coat. For 10 points, name this study of obedience by Stanley Milgram.

In 1971, this Stanford psychologist led a prison simulation in which student guards abused student prisoners and the study was ended after six days. For 10 points, name this psychologist, first name Philip.

In this 1950s study of conformity, participants judged the length of lines after confederates gave obviously wrong answers. About a third of responses conformed. For 10 points, name this experiment by Solomon Asch.

Leon Festinger developed this theory after studying a doomsday cult in When Prophecy Fails. It states that people feel discomfort when holding conflicting beliefs or when behavior contradicts beliefs, and they change attitudes to reduce it. For 10 points, name this theory.

In his conservation tasks, this psychologist showed that preoperational children think a tall thin glass holds more water than a short wide one. He also introduced the concepts of assimilation and accommodation and object permanence. For 10 points, name this Swiss developmental psychologist, first name Jean.

This Soviet psychologist introduced the zone of proximal development, the gap between what a child can do alone and with a guide. He wrote Mind in Society. For 10 points, name this theorist, first name Lev.

This theorist proposed eight psychosocial stages, each with a crisis, such as trust versus mistrust and identity versus role confusion. He coined the phrase "identity crisis." For 10 points, name this man, first name Erik.

The Heinz dilemma, about a man who steals a drug to save his dying wife, was used in this scholar's interviews with boys about moral choices. His stage theory has preconventional, conventional and postconventional levels. For 10 points, name this Harvard developmental psychologist, first name Lawrence.

This humanistic psychologist proposed a hierarchy of needs, often drawn as a pyramid, with physiological needs at the bottom and self-actualization at the top. For 10 points, name this man, first name Abraham.
This American psychologist's client-centered therapy stresses unconditional positive regard and empathy. He was a founder of humanistic psychology. For 10 points, name this man, first name Carl.

This Swiss psychiatrist split from Freud and proposed the collective unconscious containing archetypes such as the shadow and the anima. He coined the terms introvert and extravert. For 10 points, name this man, first name Carl.

In experiments on rhesus monkeys, Harry Harlow showed that infants clung to a soft terry-cloth surrogate rather than a wire one that held the milk. He concluded that affection was not just about feeding. For 10 points, what concept of need for physical closeness did he name, "comfort" through touch?

Mary Ainsworth developed this procedure to assess infant attachment, in which a baby's reactions are observed when a mother leaves and returns. It identified secure, avoidant and ambivalent styles. For 10 points, name this laboratory test.

This Harvard psychologist's 1956 paper "The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two" argued that short-term memory holds about seven items. He also coined the term chunking in this context. For 10 points, name this psychologist, first name George.

This German psychologist memorized lists of nonsense syllables and plotted a curve showing rapid forgetting that levels off. For 10 points, name this man, first name Hermann, who discovered the spacing effect.

This cognitive psychologist's studies of eyewitness testimony showed that wording, such as "smashed" versus "hit," changes recalled speed. She researches misinformation and false memories. For 10 points, name this woman, first name Elizabeth.
In 1848, an explosion drove an iron rod through the frontal lobe of this Vermont railroad foreman, who survived but whose personality changed. For 10 points, name this famous brain injury patient.

This patient, known for decades by initials, lost the ability to form new long-term memories after surgeons removed his hippocampus in 1953 to treat epilepsy. For 10 points, name this man, studied by Brenda Milner and Suzanne Corkin, whose real name was Henry Molaison.

In this task, participants name the ink color of a word like "red" printed in blue, and are slower when the word and color conflict. For 10 points, name this effect named for a psychologist John Ridley.

This school of psychology, founded by Max Wertheimer, Wolfgang Kohler and Kurt Koffka, argued that "the whole is more than the sum of its parts." It studied perception, such as the law of proximity. For 10 points, name this German school.

Martin Seligman developed this concept from experiments in which dogs that received inescapable shocks stopped trying to escape even when escape became possible. For 10 points, name this concept, linked to depression.

This French psychologist developed the first practical intelligence test in 1905 to identify children needing help in school. The Stanford revision of his test introduced the intelligence quotient. For 10 points, name this man, first name Alfred.

This psychologist's theory of multiple intelligences, from his 1983 book Frames of Mind, proposed eight or so, including musical and bodily-kinesthetic. For 10 points, name this Harvard professor, first name Howard.

This 1964 case in Queens, New York, in which a woman was killed while many neighbors reportedly did not help, inspired John Darley and Bibb Latane to study the bystander effect. For 10 points, name this victim, first name Kitty.
This model of personality traits lists openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism. Its acronym is OCEAN. For 10 points, name this model with a number in its name.

q: This French sociologist's book Distinction analyzed taste as a marker of class. He introduced the concepts of habitus, field and symbolic capital. For 10 points, name this author of Outline of a Theory of Practice, first name Pierre.

This American functionalist's AGIL scheme lists adaptation, goal attainment, integration and latency as needs every social system must meet. He wrote The Structure of Social Action. For 10 points, name this Harvard sociologist, first name Talcott.

This sociologist's world-systems theory divides the global economy into core, semi-periphery and periphery. His multivolume The Modern World-System traces capitalism from the sixteenth century. For 10 points, name this man, first name Immanuel.

Harold Garfinkel founded this approach, studying the methods ordinary people use to make sense of social life, with "breaching experiments" that disrupt everyday norms. For 10 points, name this approach whose name combines Greek words for people and methods.

This Italian Marxist, writing in prison, developed the idea of cultural hegemony: that the ruling class maintains power through consent and shaping common sense. His Prison Notebooks were published after his death. For 10 points, name this man, first name Antonio.

This French thinker analyzed Jeremy Bentham's circular prison design in Discipline and Punish as a symbol of modern surveillance. He also wrote The History of Sexuality. For 10 points, name this man, first name Michel.

In a 1973 paper, this Stanford sociologist argued that acquaintances may be more useful than close friends for finding jobs, because they provide new information. For 10 points, name this paper "The Strength of Weak Ties" by Mark Granovetter.

This sociologist's The Power Elite argued that military, corporate and political leaders dominate American decision making. For 10 points, name this author whose The Sociological Imagination appeared in 1959, first name Charles Wright.

In this 1987 book, William Julius Wilson argued that deindustrialization and the flight of middle-class families left inner-city neighborhoods isolated. For 10 points, name this book titled for people at the bottom of society.

This sociologist's books The Managed Heart and The Second Shift examined work and family. She coined "emotional labor," studying flight attendants. For 10 points, name this Berkeley scholar, first name Arlie.

This legal scholar coined the term "intersectionality" in 1989 to describe how race and gender discrimination overlap, using the case of Emma DeGraffenreid against General Motors. For 10 points, name this woman, first name Kimberle.

Peter Berger and Thomas Luckmann wrote this 1966 book arguing that what people take as reality is built through shared interaction and habit. For 10 points, name this book, whose title contains the phrase "social construction."
Robert Michels formulated this "law" in his book Political Parties, claiming that all organizations, even democratic ones, inevitably become dominated by a small elite. For 10 points, name this law.

Weber described three types of legitimate authority: traditional, rational-legal and this type, based on an individual's exceptional personal qualities. For 10 points, name this kind of authority, exemplified by prophets.
Weber introduced this concept, a German word meaning "understanding," for interpreting the subjective meanings people attach to their actions. For 10 points, name this interpretive method.

Robert Merton coined this phrase for a false definition of a situation that evokes behavior making the false idea come true, as when a rumor of a bank failure causes a run on the bank. For 10 points, name this prophecy.

This British sociologist developed structuration theory and wrote The Consequences of Modernity and The Third Way. For 10 points, name this man, first name Anthony, who was director of the London School of Economics.

This German sociologist's Risk Society argued that modern societies increasingly face hazards produced by their own technologies. He also wrote of the "second modernity" and reflexive modernization. For 10 points, name this man, first name Ulrich.

This Polish-born sociologist wrote Liquid Modernity, describing a society in which social forms melt quickly. He also wrote on the Holocaust and modernity. For 10 points, name this man, first name Zygmunt.

Kingsley Davis and Wilbert Moore argued that social stratification is functional because it motivates talented people to fill important roles. For 10 points, name this broader thesis, a functionalist defense of inequality, named for its two authors.

This sociologist wrote Unequal Childhoods, contrasting "concerted cultivation" in middle-class families with the "accomplishment of natural growth" in working-class families. For 10 points, name this sociologist, first name Annette.

Elliot Liebow's classic ethnography Tally's Corner studied Black men gathered at one of these places, in Washington, D.C. For 10 points, name this kind of neighborhood spot, an urban street-corner setting.

This Frenchman's 1925 essay The Gift argued that gift exchange creates obligations to give, receive and reciprocate, using examples from Polynesia and the Pacific Northwest. For 10 points, name this nephew of Durkheim, first name Marcel.

Douglas Massey and Nancy Denton described this arrangement of residential separation by race in their 1993 book American Apartheid. For 10 points, name this term for the separation of groups into different neighborhoods.
This term, coined by Robert Merton, names a group that individuals compare themselves to when evaluating their own situation, even if they do not belong to it. For 10 points, name this kind of group.

Elton Mayo's studies at a Western Electric plant near Chicago led to the naming of this effect, in which people change their behavior because they know they are being observed. For 10 points, name this effect named for a factory.

This model describes how societies move from high birth and death rates to low ones as they industrialize, passing through four or five stages. Warren Thompson first described it. For 10 points, name this demographic model.

Max Weber used this term for a mental construct that accentuates the typical features of a social phenomenon, such as bureaucracy, for comparison. It does not represent moral perfection. For 10 points, name this methodological tool, "type" preceded by a word for a perfect model.

This English cleric's 1798 Essay on the Principle of Population argued that population grows geometrically while food supply grows arithmetically, leading to "positive checks" like famine. For 10 points, name this man, first name Thomas.

The sociologist Ruth Glass coined this word in 1964 to describe how middle-class people were moving into working-class areas of London, raising rents and displacing residents. For 10 points, name this process, also seen in urban neighborhoods across America.

q: This American philosopher's A Theory of Justice proposed that principles of justice would be chosen by people behind a "veil of ignorance," not knowing their own place in society. His two principles include the difference principle. For 10 points, name this Harvard philosopher, first name John.

This Irish-born British statesman's Reflections on the Revolution in France criticized the French Revolution and defended tradition and gradual reform. He is often considered a founder of modern conservatism. For 10 points, name this man, first name Edmund.

In his essay "Perpetual Peace," this German philosopher argued that republican constitutions, federations of free states and universal hospitality could end war. This idea inspired democratic peace theory. For 10 points, name this author of Critique of Pure Reason.

In this 1992 book, Francis Fukuyama argued that liberal democracy might be the endpoint of humanity's ideological evolution. It expanded an essay with a similar title. For 10 points, name this book, whose title also names a "last man."

Anthony Downs's An Economic Theory of Democracy popularized this theorem, which states that in a one-dimensional policy space, majority-rule outcomes converge on the preferences of the voter in the center. For 10 points, name this theorem about the typical voter.

This political scientist's The Logic of Collective Action argued that large groups face a free-rider problem and that small groups or selective incentives organize more easily. For 10 points, name this author, first name Mancur.

Kenneth Waltz's Theory of International Politics founded this school, which argues that the structure of the international system, not human nature, explains state behavior. It is also called structural realism. For 10 points, name this theory.
This University of Chicago professor's The Tragedy of Great Power Politics defended offensive realism, claiming that states maximize relative power. For 10 points, name this author, first name John.

This Yale political scientist coined the term "polyarchy" for real-world democracies in works such as Who Governs? and A Preface to Democratic Theory. He studied New Haven. For 10 points, name this author, first name Robert.

Arend Lijphart's work on this form of democracy, found in places such as Belgium and Switzerland, stresses power sharing among social segments through grand coalitions and mutual vetoes. For 10 points, name this type of power-sharing democracy.

This 1962 Supreme Court case, from Tennessee, held that federal courts could hear challenges to legislative malapportionment, leading to "one person, one vote." For 10 points, name this case against a Tennessee Secretary of State.

In this 1964 Supreme Court case, Justice Hugo Black wrote that congressional districts must have roughly equal populations. For 10 points, name this case from Georgia, named for a man who sued over his district.

Benedict Anderson's 1983 book argued that nations are "imagined communities" made possible by print capitalism, such as newspapers and novels in vernacular languages. For 10 points, name this book's two-word subject, a type of social group larger than a village.

This German jurist and political theorist wrote The Concept of the Political, defining politics as the distinction between friend and enemy. He also wrote that the sovereign is he who decides on the exception. For 10 points, name this man, first name Carl.

This Oxford philosopher's essay "Two Concepts of Liberty" distinguished negative liberty, freedom from interference, from positive liberty, freedom to be one's own master. For 10 points, name this Russian-born thinker, first name Isaiah.

This Prussian chancellor, who unified Germany in 1871 through wars with Denmark, Austria and France, practiced "realpolitik," putting pragmatic power politics ahead of ideology. For 10 points, name this man, first name Otto von.

This Austrian foreign minister presided over the 1814 and 1815 Congress of Vienna and was the leading architect of the conservative Concert of Europe. For 10 points, name this man, first name Klemens von.

In this passage of Thucydides's History of the Peloponnesian War, Athenian envoys tell the people of a small island that "the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must." For 10 points, name this episode, named for the island of Melos.

This Greek historian argued in Book VI of his Histories that the Roman Republic was stable because it combined monarchy, aristocracy and democracy through consuls, Senate and assemblies. For 10 points, name this author, whose theory of mixed government influenced Montesquieu and the framers.

This Harvard professor's 1996 book predicted that post-Cold War conflicts would occur along cultural fault lines among large civilizations, such as Western, Islamic and Sinic. For 10 points, name this author of The Clash of Civilizations, first name Samuel.

This phenomenon, described by Robert Putnam in a 1988 article, models international negotiation as a game played at both the domestic and international levels. For 10 points, name this model, whose name includes two "levels."

This eighteenth-century French marquis showed that majority rule can produce cycles in which A beats B, B beats C, and C beats A. For 10 points, name this paradox of voting named for a philosopher-mathematician, the Marquis de Condorcet.

This Roman statesman and orator's De Re Publica described the republic as the "thing of the people" and praised a mixed constitution. His Catilinarian orations denounced a conspirator. For 10 points, name this man, an opponent of Mark Antony.
This 1919 treaty ended World War I with Germany, imposing reparations and a "war guilt" clause, and created the League of Nations. For 10 points, name this treaty signed in the Hall of Mirrors.

This 1803 land deal, negotiated in Paris by Robert Livingston and James Monroe, doubled the size of the United States and was agreed to by Napoleon for about fifteen million dollars. Thomas Jefferson worried about its constitutionality. For 10 points, name this purchase from France.

This 1973 law, passed over President Nixon's veto, requires the president to notify Congress within 48 hours of sending troops into hostilities and limits deployments to 60 days without approval. For 10 points, name this law about presidential military powers.

Under this principle, found in the Supremacy Clause of Article VI, federal law prevails over conflicting state law. For 10 points, name this doctrine, established in McCulloch v. Maryland and Gibbons v. Ogden.

In this 1966 Supreme Court case, Chief Justice Earl Warren's opinion required police to inform suspects of their right to remain silent and to an attorney before custodial questioning. For 10 points, name this case named for an Arizona man, which gave rise to a famous "warning."

This Chinese leader founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 after the Communist victory over the Nationalists. His writings are collected in the Little Red Book. For 10 points, name this chairman, first name Mao.

This 1951 book by an exiled German-born Jewish thinker analyzed Nazism and Stalinism as unprecedented regimes that use terror and ideology to dominate every part of life. For 10 points, name this work by Hannah Arendt, whose title names an "origins" of a form of total rule.

q: This British anthropologist's Witchcraft, Oracles and Magic among the Azande showed that beliefs in witchcraft form a coherent system of explanation. He also studied the Nuer of Sudan and wrote about their segmentary lineage system. For 10 points, name this Oxford scholar, first name E. E.

This British anthropologist's Purity and Danger argued that ideas of pollution and "matter out of place" reflect a society's categories. She analyzed the dietary rules of Leviticus. For 10 points, name this author, first name Mary.

This Australian-born archaeologist coined the term "Neolithic Revolution" and wrote Man Makes Himself and What Happened in History. He was a Marxist who excavated at Skara Brae. For 10 points, name this scholar, first name V. Gordon.

This American archaeologist founded processual archaeology, which stressed scientific hypothesis testing and the study of ecological adaptation. He conducted ethnoarchaeology among the Nunamiut. For 10 points, name this author of New Perspectives in Archaeology, first name Lewis.

This British archaeologist, an advocate of post-processual archaeology, has directed excavations at Catalhoyuk in Turkey since the 1990s. His reflexive approach emphasizes meaning and symbolism. For 10 points, name this scholar, first name Ian.

This German businessman turned archaeologist claimed to have found Troy at Hisarlik in the 1870s, and he also dug at Mycenae. His methods were destructive. For 10 points, name this man, first name Heinrich.
This English archaeologist excavated the Minoan palace at Knossos on Crete beginning in 1900 and named the Minoan civilization after a legendary king. For 10 points, name this man, first name Arthur.
In 1922, this British archaeologist, funded by Lord Carnarvon, discovered the nearly intact tomb of Tutankhamun in the Valley of the Kings. For 10 points, name this man, first name Howard.
In 1947, this Norwegian explorer sailed a balsa raft from Peru to Polynesia to argue that South Americans could have settled Polynesia. For 10 points, name this man, who named his raft Kon-Tiki.
This extinct hominin was found on the Indonesian island of Flores in 2003. Nicknamed the "hobbit," it stood about a meter tall. For 10 points, name this species, named for its island home.

This group of extinct archaic humans was identified in 2010 from DNA extracted from a finger bone found in a Siberian cave. Modern Melanesians carry some of their DNA. For 10 points, name this group named for a cave in the Altai Mountains.

This hominin genus, whose name means "southern ape," includes Lucy. A more robust genus found in East and South Africa that lived alongside it is Paranthropus. For 10 points, name the genus of Lucy and the Taung Child.

This site in Georgia's Caucasus region has produced some of the oldest hominin fossils outside Africa, dated to about 1.8 million years ago. For 10 points, name this site in the Republic of Georgia, home of "Homo georgicus" skulls.

This is the hypothesis that anatomically modern humans arose in Africa and spread outward, replacing other hominins. It is supported by mitochondrial DNA studies of "Eve." For 10 points, name this model, opposed to multiregional evolution.

Stone tools associated with these early Americans, characterized by fluted spear points, were first found near a New Mexico town in the 1930s. They date to about 13,000 years ago. For 10 points, name this culture named for that town, a "Clovis" culture.

Anthropologists propose that the first Americans crossed this former land bridge between Siberia and Alaska during the Ice Age, when sea levels were lower. For 10 points, name this land bridge, named for a strait.
This Chilean site, dated to at least 14,500 years ago, is evidence for people in South America before the Clovis culture. For 10 points, name this archaeological site excavated by Tom Dillehay.

Cave paintings of horses, bison and aurochs, made about 17,000 years ago, were found by teenagers in 1940 in this cave in the Dordogne region of France. For 10 points, name this cave, often called the "Sistine Chapel of prehistory."

This small limestone figurine, about 25,000 years old, shows a woman with exaggerated breasts and belly. It was found in Austria. For 10 points, name this prehistoric art object, named for the site where it was found.

This American anthropologist coined the term "cultural ecology" and studied the Shoshone, arguing that environment shapes culture. His theory of multilinear evolution contrasted with unilinear evolution. For 10 points, name this author of Theory of Culture Change, first name Julian.

This University of Chicago anthropologist's Stone Age Economics argued that hunter-gatherers were the "original affluent society." He also studied Hawaiian history and the apotheosis of Captain Cook. For 10 points, name this man, first name Marshall.

This American anthropologist's theory of cultural materialism, in books such as Cows, Pigs, Wars, and Witches, explains practices like the Hindu sacred cow in terms of material conditions. For 10 points, name this author, first name Marvin.

Richard Lee studied this group of foragers in the Kalahari Desert of Botswana and Namibia, who speak a language with click consonants. For 10 points, name this group, whose name begins with a click symbol, also called the Ju/'hoansi.

This American anthropologist's The Forest People described the Mbuti Pygmies of the Ituri Forest, while The Mountain People described the Ik of Uganda. For 10 points, name this author, first name Colin.

Alfred Kroeber and Clyde Kluckhohn compiled hundreds of definitions of this central term of anthropology. Franz Boas's students emphasized that it is learned and shared, not biological. For 10 points, name this term.

These remains of a body found in a peat bog in Denmark, such as Tollund Man, are called by this term because bog conditions preserve skin and hair. For 10 points, name these preserved bodies of the Iron Age.

In 1991, hikers in the Alps found this Copper Age man, nicknamed "the Iceman," whose body was preserved in a glacier. He lived about 5,300 years ago. For 10 points, name this mummy, named for a mountain range between Austria and Italy.

This 1996 discovery in Washington State of a skeleton about 8,500 years old led to a legal fight over whether scientists could study it or Native American tribes could rebury it. For 10 points, name this skeleton, named for a town.

This 1990 United States law requires federal agencies and museums receiving federal funds to return certain Native American human remains and cultural items to descendants and tribes. For 10 points, name this law, abbreviated NAGPRA.

Called "Ardi" by her discoverers, the skeleton of this 4.4-million-year-old hominin was described in 2009 from Ethiopia's Middle Awash. It had a grasping big toe but also walked upright. For 10 points, name this genus with a name based on an Afar word for "ground floor."

Anthropologists distinguish between emic and etic perspectives, terms coined by Kenneth Pike from phonemic and phonetic. In the emic approach, researchers describe a culture from this viewpoint. For 10 points, name this point of view, that of those inside the culture.
